readings.title: The blue bag
paragraphs: Mia is at the airport with her father. Her ticket and passport are in a small blue bag. They have two bags: Mia's bag is blue, and her father's bag is black. A woman near the door has a blue bag too. Mia puts her bag on a chair and goes to buy water. Her father stays near the chair.

When Mia comes back, the chair is empty. She looks at the woman, but the woman's bag has a white star on it. Mia's bag has no star. Then her father smiles. He has Mia's bag under his coat. They walk to their gate together.

questions.question: Where is Mia's passport at the start?
questions.explanation: Paszport i bilet są w małej niebieskiej torbie Mii.
questions.evidence: Her ticket and passport are in a small blue bag.

questions.question: How is the woman's bag different?
questions.explanation: Kolor jest ten sam, ale gwiazdka odróżnia torby.
questions.evidence: the woman's bag has a white star on it.

questions.question: Who has Mia's bag at the end?
questions.explanation: Zaimek „he” odnosi się do ojca, który właśnie się uśmiecha.
questions.evidence: He has Mia's bag under his coat.

readings.title: Lunch after the rush
paragraphs: Leo works in a small restaurant. He starts at ten in the morning. At twelve, many people come for lunch. Leo brings soup, bread, and water to their tables. He is hungry, but he does not eat with the customers. He eats when the restaurant is quiet.

Today, a family leaves at two. Leo cleans their table and sits near the window. The cook brings him a bowl of soup. There is no bread left, so Leo has rice with his soup. His friend calls and asks him to meet at three. Leo says yes. He finishes work at half past two.

questions.question: When does Leo eat today?
questions.explanation: Najpierw wychodzi rodzina, potem Leo siada do posiłku.
questions.evidence: a family leaves at two. Leo cleans their table and sits near the window.

questions.question: Why does he eat rice?
questions.explanation: Ryż zastępuje pieczywo, którego już nie ma.
questions.evidence: There is no bread left, so Leo has rice with his soup.

questions.question: Can Leo meet his friend at three?
options: No, he starts work at three
Yes, his work ends before three
questions.explanation: Half past two to 14:30, czyli przed 15:00.
questions.evidence: He finishes work at half past two.

glossary.translation: pozostały (no bread left = nie ma już chleba)
wpół do (half past two = wpół do trzeciej)

readings.title: A card for Saturday
paragraphs: Ella wants a book about animals. She goes to the library on Saturday morning. Her brother Max comes with her. He wants a book about trains. Ella has a library card, but Max does not have one. The woman at the desk gives Max a form. He writes his name and address on it.

Ella finds two books about animals. One is very big, and the other is small. She chooses the small book because it fits in her bag. Max gets his new card and a book about trains. They sit at a table for ten minutes. Then they take their books home.

questions.question: Who needs a new card?
questions.explanation: Kartę ma już Ella; formularz wypełnia Max.
questions.evidence: Ella has a library card, but Max does not have one.

questions.question: Why does Ella choose the small book?
options: It is the only book there
It has her name in it
questions.explanation: Decyduje rozmiar książki, a nie inna tematyka.
questions.evidence: She chooses the small book because it fits in her bag.

questions.question: Where do they go at the end?
questions.explanation: Na końcu zabierają książki do domu.
questions.evidence: Then they take their books home.

readings.title: Water for the garden
paragraphs: Ben and his grandmother have a little garden behind their house. There are tomatoes, flowers, and a young tree. Ben waters the flowers every evening. His grandmother waters the tomatoes. The tree needs water only twice a week.

On Monday, Ben comes home late. The flowers are dry, but the ground near the tree is wet. His grandmother has already watered the tree. Ben fills a green bucket and waters the flowers. He does not give the tree more water. After that, they sit outside and look at the garden. Ben picks one red tomato for his dinner. The other tomatoes are still green.

questions.question: What does Ben usually water?
questions.explanation: Codziennym zadaniem Bena są kwiaty.
questions.evidence: Ben waters the flowers every evening.

questions.question: Why does Ben not water the tree on Monday?
options: It is not in the garden
His grandmother wants to cut it down
questions.explanation: Babcia zrobiła to wcześniej; ziemia przy drzewie jest mokra.
questions.evidence: His grandmother has already watered the tree.

questions.question: How many tomatoes does Ben pick?
questions.explanation: Zrywa jeden czerwony pomidor, pozostałe są zielone.
questions.evidence: Ben picks one red tomato for his dinner.

readings.title: The room with the red door
paragraphs: Nora has a new job in an office. On her first day, she arrives at eight. Her manager, Sam, is in a meeting. A woman at the front desk shows Nora a small room with a red door. There is a computer on the desk and a jacket on the chair. The jacket belongs to Sam, but the desk is for Nora.
Nora puts her own coat on a hook and turns on the computer. At nine, Sam comes in. He takes his jacket and gives Nora a notebook. They go to the kitchen for coffee. Then Nora returns to her new desk.

questions.question: Where is Sam when Nora arrives?
questions.explanation: Sam jest na spotkaniu, dlatego Norę wprowadza inna osoba.

readings.title: A small favor
paragraphs: Mia has a new job. Her office is near a bank. Today she has no pen. She asks Tom, “Can I borrow your pen?” Tom says yes. Mia uses the pen and gives it back. After work, they have coffee.

questions.question: What does Mia need?
questions.explanation: Mia nie ma długopisu, więc prosi Toma o pożyczenie.

readings.title: Lunch for two
paragraphs: Ben goes to a small restaurant with Ana. Ana has soup, but Ben wants a sandwich. The waiter recommends the cheese sandwich. Ben orders it and shares it with Ana. They like the food and walk home together.

readings.title: A different gate
paragraphs: Daniel reached the airport two hours before his flight. His boarding pass said Gate 12, so he bought a sandwich near that gate. While he was eating, he received a message from his sister. She asked him to buy a small gift at the airport store. Daniel checked the time and decided that he had enough time.

The store was only five minutes away. He chose a book and waited to pay. Just then, he heard an announcement about his flight. It was leaving from Gate 20 instead of Gate 12. The departure time had not changed. Daniel left the book on a shelf and walked quickly to the new gate. A staff member checked his passport there. He boarded with the last group of passengers and sent his sister a message: the gift would have to wait until his next visit.

questions.question: Why did Daniel go to the store?
options: His gate was inside the store
His sister asked for a gift
questions.explanation: Wizyta w sklepie wynikała z prośby siostry.

questions.question: What changed about the flight?

questions.question: Did Daniel buy the book?

No, he left it before paying
Yes, he paid at the gate
questions.explanation: Zostawił książkę, żeby dotrzeć do nowej bramki.
questions.evidence: Daniel left the book on a shelf and walked quickly to the new gate.

questions.question: What happened in the end?
options: He caught the flight without a gift
questions.explanation: Zdążył wejść na pokład, ale nie kupił prezentu.
questions.evidence: He boarded with the last group of passengers

readings.title: The table by the window
paragraphs: Ruby booked a table for six people at a restaurant. She asked for a table by the window because her grandfather liked watching the river. When they arrived, the waiter showed them a table in the middle of the room. Ruby explained what she had requested. The waiter checked the booking and apologized. The window table was ready, but it had only five chairs.

Ruby's cousin was not coming because she was ill, so there were only five people in the group. They moved to the window table and ordered lunch. Ruby's grandfather chose fish, but the waiter said it would take twenty minutes longer than the other meals. He chose pasta instead. Nobody was in a hurry, but he wanted to eat with everyone else. After lunch, the family took a photo by the river. Ruby sent it to her cousin with a message: they would visit again together.

questions.question: Why did Ruby want a window table?
options: The middle of the room was closed
Her grandfather liked the river view
questions.explanation: Prośba dotyczyła widoku, a nie ceny czy zamkniętej sali.
questions.evidence: her grandfather liked watching the river.

questions.question: Why were five chairs enough?
options: A child stood by the window
questions.explanation: Rezerwacja była dla sześciu osób, lecz przyszło pięć.
questions.evidence: Ruby's cousin was not coming because she was ill

questions.question: Why did the grandfather choose pasta?
options: He wanted to eat with the others
The waiter brought the wrong dish
questions.explanation: Nie brak czasu, lecz wspólny posiłek zdecydował o zmianie zamówienia.
questions.evidence: he wanted to eat with everyone else.

questions.question: Who received the photo?
questions.explanation: Kuzynka nie uczestniczyła w obiedzie, więc dostała zdjęcie.
questions.evidence: Ruby sent it to her cousin

readings.title: A useful mistake
paragraphs: On Tuesday, Omar rode his bike to work. Near the park, he heard a strange sound from the back wheel. He stopped and called a repair shop. The mechanic said she could look at the bike that afternoon. Omar locked it outside a cafe and took the bus to his office.

At lunchtime, he realized that he had given the mechanic the wrong street name. He called again and corrected it. The mechanic laughed and said there were two cafes with the same name in town. She had not left the shop yet, so the mistake did not waste her trip. Later, she collected the bike and repaired it. Omar picked it up after work. The repair cost less than he expected because the wheel did not need replacing. He saved the shop's number in his phone and wrote down the correct address of the cafe too.

questions.question: How did Omar finish his journey to work?
questions.explanation: Rower zostawił pod kawiarnią; do pracy pojechał autobusem.
questions.evidence: took the bus to his office.

questions.question: What information did he correct?
questions.explanation: Pomyłka dotyczyła ulicy, na której stał rower.

questions.explanation: Naprawa nie wymagała zakupu nowego koła.

readings.title: The earlier appointment
paragraphs: Clara had an appointment at a clinic on Friday afternoon. On Thursday, the receptionist called and offered her a time that morning instead. Another patient had canceled. Clara agreed because she wanted to ask the doctor about a cough before a weekend trip. She told her manager that she would arrive at work late.

At the clinic, Clara waited beside a man who was reading a newspaper. He had arrived before her, but the nurse called Clara first. The man was waiting for a different doctor. Clara's doctor examined her and told her to rest. He did not say that she needed to cancel her trip, but he suggested avoiding long walks. Clara and her friend had planned a full day in the mountains. They changed that plan and booked a quiet place near a lake. Clara was glad she had accepted the earlier appointment: now she had time to organize a gentler weekend.

questions.question: Why could Clara see the doctor earlier?
options: The clinic opened a new building
Her friend gave her an appointment
questions.explanation: Zwolnił się termin innego pacjenta.

questions.question: Why was Clara called before the man?

questions.question: What did the doctor suggest?

questions.question: How did Clara change her weekend?
options: She moved the trip to Friday
She went alone to the mountains
questions.explanation: Zmieniła charakter wypoczynku, a nie zrezygnowała z niego.

readings.title: The note on the fridge
paragraphs: Three students shared an apartment. Every Sunday, they wrote a shopping list on the fridge. This week, Nina added milk and apples. Josh added bread. Amir saw the list on Monday morning and bought all three things on his way home from class. He put the receipt beside the list so they could share the cost.

That evening, Nina came home with another bag of apples. She had seen a message from Josh about buying bread, but she had not checked the fridge. At first, she thought Amir had forgotten to tell everyone about his shopping. Then she noticed his message in their group chat. Her phone had been turned off during class. They now had too many apples, but nobody was angry. Amir suggested making a cake. After dinner, they agreed on a new rule: the person who finished the shopping would cross the items off the list as well as send a message.

options: He sent it the next day
Amir sent it to Josh only

The hotel is next to the river, so they decide to walk along the bank before dinner.

readings.title: The connection nobody missed
paragraphs: When their first flight landed late, Priya and her colleague assumed they had missed their connection. The departure screen showed that the next plane was still on time, but its gate was on the other side of the terminal. They had twenty minutes, and Priya's colleague suggested running straight there. Priya wanted to speak to an airline employee first. Her colleague thought this would waste the few minutes they had left.

The employee checked their boarding passes and explained that the connecting flight was waiting for several passengers from the late arrival. However, she also noticed that their checked luggage had been booked to a different airport in the same city. Running to the gate would not have solved that problem. She called the baggage team, corrected the destination, and gave the passengers a printed confirmation.

They reached the gate while the last group was boarding. On the plane, Priya's colleague admitted that stopping had been the better decision. Priya was less certain. If the employee had not been available, she might have chosen differently. What mattered, she said, was asking the right person rather than simply moving faster. When they arrived, both suitcases were on the correct baggage carousel. Their meeting was the following morning, so they still had the evening to prepare.

The employee told him to run
He believed very little boarding time remained
He knew the baggage was at the wrong airport

questions.evidence: They had twenty minutes

questions.question: What unexpected problem did the employee find?

The bags had the wrong destination airport

readings.title: A quieter kind of success
paragraphs: A neighborhood restaurant introduced a special lunch menu to attract office workers. The owner, Rosa, expected customers to care mainly about speed and price. For the first week, the kitchen prepared three dishes in advance, and the staff promised that every meal would reach the table within ten minutes. Sales increased, but several customers left without ordering. Rosa assumed the menu was too limited.

Instead of immediately adding more dishes, she asked people near the entrance why they were leaving. Some had only wanted a coffee, but others said the music made conversation difficult. One customer regularly met a client over lunch and needed somewhere quiet. Rosa lowered the volume in the back room and stopped seating large groups there. She kept the same lunch menu and prices.

A month later, the quieter tables were usually full. Meals there took slightly longer because customers stayed to talk, so those tables served fewer people each afternoon. Even so, the restaurant earned more from the room because guests often ordered desserts and returned the following week. Rosa kept the faster service at the front for customers with short breaks. The result did not show that speed was unimportant. It showed that different customers used the same restaurant for different reasons, and one arrangement could not satisfy them all.

There were not enough menu choices

options: The atmosphere in part of the restaurant

questions.question: What is the main lesson?

questions.explanation: Wniosek dotyczy różnych potrzeb, a nie całkowitego odrzucenia szybkości obsługi.
questions.evidence: different customers used the same restaurant for different reasons

readings.title: The repair that took two Saturdays
paragraphs: Lena took an old radio to a volunteer repair club. It had belonged to her grandfather, and she hoped to use it in her kitchen. At the entrance, a sign warned visitors that volunteers could not promise to repair every object. They would also ask owners to stay and help rather than simply leave their things and return later. Lena had expected a free repair service, so this surprised her.

A volunteer named Marcus showed her how to open the case safely. They found a damaged switch, but the club did not have a replacement. Lena offered to buy a new radio and give up on the old one. Marcus explained that a suitable switch would be inexpensive, although finding the right size might take time. He wrote down the measurements, and Lena ordered the part that evening.

The following Saturday, they fitted the switch together. The radio worked, but the sound was still not perfect. Marcus offered to investigate further. Lena decided it was good enough for the kitchen and took it home. She had spent more time than she expected, but she now understood how to check a simple fault. A month later, she returned with a broken lamp and the correct replacement cable. This time, she brought her younger brother because he wanted to learn too.

questions.question: How was the club different from Lena's expectation?
options: Owners took part in the repairs
Visitors had to work there every week

questions.evidence: ask owners to stay and help

questions.question: Why was a second visit necessary?

Lena had not brought the radio
The correct switch was not available
questions.explanation: Brak części wymusił zamówienie i ponowną wizytę.

questions.evidence: Lena decided it was good enough for the kitchen

questions.question: What does Lena's later visit suggest?

She had gained confidence and wanted to share the experience

questions.explanation: Przygotowała część samodzielnie i przyprowadziła brata; nie ma mowy o zdobyciu zawodu.

readings.title: The shorter route
paragraphs: Four friends planned a long walk through the hills. They had studied a map and chosen a route that usually took five hours. The weather forecast showed light rain in the morning and sunshine later. Because everyone wanted to reach a small village for lunch, they agreed to leave early. By nine o'clock, however, they were still at the station: one train had been canceled, and the next was crowded.

When they finally arrived at the start of the trail, Noah suggested taking a shorter route. It would miss the highest viewpoint but pass an old bridge and reach the village before the cafe closed. The others were disappointed. They had looked forward to the view, and the sky was now clear. One friend argued that they could walk faster and still complete the original route.

Noah pointed out that walking faster would leave little time for breaks. They had different levels of fitness, and the last bus home would not wait for them. After checking the map again, the group chose the shorter path. They reached the village comfortably and even had time to talk to the cafe owner about local history. On the bus home, they agreed to attempt the longer route another day. Changing the plan had not been their first choice, but it had kept the afternoon enjoyable for everyone.

questions.question: What mainly caused the change of plan?
questions.explanation: Zdecydowało opóźnienie dojazdu; podczas rozmowy o trasie niebo było już czyste.
questions.evidence: one train had been canceled

questions.question: What would they miss on the shorter route?

He had already seen the village

questions.question: How did the friends feel about the final choice?

questions.explanation: Nie był to plan pierwotny, ale pozwolił wszystkim przyjemnie spędzić czas.
questions.evidence: it had kept the afternoon enjoyable for everyone.

readings.title: A question before opening
paragraphs: On his first morning at a bookstore, Ethan was asked to prepare an online order. The customer had bought a travel guide and a notebook. Ethan found both items and was about to wrap them when he noticed that the guide described the previous year's train schedules. A newer edition stood on the same shelf, but it cost more. The order clearly named the older edition.

Ethan could have followed the order exactly and finished the task quickly. Instead, he asked his supervisor whether they should contact the customer. She said that some customers deliberately bought older guides because they were cheaper, while others did not realize there was a difference. She helped Ethan write a short message explaining both options without recommending the more expensive book automatically.

The customer replied before the shop opened. She was collecting old editions for a research project and wanted the exact book she had ordered. Ethan wrapped it and added a note confirming the edition. His question had not led to a different sale, but the supervisor was pleased. The aim, she explained, was not always to change a customer's mind. Sometimes checking an unusual detail was simply a way to make sure the shop had understood the request. Later that week, Ethan noticed a similar issue in another order and knew whom to ask.

options: The shop had no newer guide
questions.explanation: Wątpliwość dotyczyła aktualności przewodnika, nie braku produktu.
questions.evidence: the guide described the previous year's train schedules.

questions.question: What did the supervisor recommend?
options: Send the expensive guide for free
Explain the options without assuming what the customer wanted
questions.explanation: Chodziło o sprawdzenie potrzeby klientki, a nie automatyczne zwiększenie sprzedaży.
questions.evidence: explaining both options without recommending the more expensive book automatically.

questions.question: Why did the customer want the old guide?
options: She could not afford any newer books

readings.title: The quiet terminal experiment
paragraphs: For years, announcements at Westhaven Airport had repeated information already displayed on screens. Travelers complained about the noise, while staff argued that frequent announcements prevented passengers from missing flights. When the airport tested a quieter terminal, managers agreed to announce only urgent changes and final boarding calls. Routine information would remain on screens and in the airport app. The trial lasted six weeks, covering both busy and quiet periods.

At first, the results appeared straightforward. Noise complaints fell sharply, and surveys showed that most passengers preferred the calmer atmosphere. Yet the airport's accessibility team warned against treating the average score as the whole story. Some passengers could not comfortably read distant screens. Others had phones without an internet connection or found the app difficult to use. These groups were small in the survey, partly because the questionnaire itself was offered through the app.

Rather than abandon the trial, the airport installed additional screens at sitting height and introduced clearly marked assistance points. Staff also offered passengers a choice of receiving essential updates by text message. The number of missed flights did not increase during the second half of the trial, although managers admitted that six weeks was too short to judge every seasonal situation.

The final report recommended keeping the quieter policy with the new support measures. Its authors resisted describing the experiment as a simple victory for technology. The app had helped some travelers, but the improvement depended equally on physical signs and available staff. An airport could become quieter without becoming less informative, they concluded, provided that information reached passengers in more than one way.

readings.title: A label is only a beginning
paragraphs: A restaurant chain decided to mark dishes that could be prepared without certain common ingredients. The new menu used simple symbols, and managers expected ordering to become easier. During training, however, a chef pointed out that changing an ingredient was not the same as preventing all contact with it. A sauce could be left off a plate, for example, while the equipment used to prepare the meal might still have touched that sauce earlier.

The company revised the wording before printing the menus. Instead of making a broad promise, the symbols invited customers to discuss their needs with staff. Some managers worried that this extra conversation would slow service and make the labels seem less useful. The chef argued that a quick but misleading answer was worse than a slightly longer, accurate one. Staff were given a list of preparation procedures and told whom to consult when they were uncertain.

After three months, the chain reviewed customer comments and a sample of orders. Fewer meals had to be returned because of misunderstood requests. The review did not prove that every kitchen followed every procedure perfectly, and the company continued its inspections. It did suggest that the conversations were helping customers make informed choices.

The most useful feedback came from a customer who rarely ordered the same dish twice. She said the symbols helped her begin a conversation, not avoid one. What reassured her was a server who could explain the limits of the information and check with the kitchen. The chain kept the labels, but its next training session focused less on remembering symbols and more on asking clear questions and admitting uncertainty.

readings.title: What the shorter week changed
paragraphs: A design company tested a four-day working week without reducing salaries. Before the trial, its director predicted that a longer weekend would make employees more productive. The staff were enthusiastic, but the team responsible for customer support was worried. Clients would still expect replies on Fridays, and simply closing the office could shift work into an unpaid day at home.

The company therefore arranged different days off for different teams. It also shortened regular meetings, stopped requiring two managers to approve small purchases, and introduced a shared record of decisions. These changes were meant to prevent the same work from being squeezed into fewer hours. Employees recorded both their official working time and any time spent checking messages outside it.

At the end of the trial, completed projects and customer satisfaction had remained stable. Staff reported feeling less tired, and after-hours messaging had fallen. The director initially described the result as proof that four days were enough for any office. An internal analyst objected. The trial had combined several changes, so it was impossible to know how much of the benefit came from the extra day off rather than the simpler procedures. The company also had a relatively predictable workload during those months.

They decided to keep the shorter week, but the public report used more careful language. It described what had worked in that company and listed the conditions that had helped. Another business might need a different schedule, the report noted. The director accepted the revision. A less dramatic claim would be less useful in an advertisement, but more useful to employers deciding whether to run their own trial.

readings.title: The cleanup that changed direction
paragraphs: Every spring, residents of Brookfield collected litter from the riverbank. The event was popular, and photos of full trash bags appeared in the local newspaper. After several years, volunteer organizer Mei began to question what those photos actually showed. A large collection could mean that the team had worked hard, but it could also mean that more waste was reaching the river. The same figure could tell two very different stories.

Mei asked volunteers to record the kinds of litter they found and the places where it collected. Many assumed visitors to the riverside park were responsible. The records showed plenty of food packaging, but a surprisingly large amount of material came from construction sites upstream. Heavy rain carried it through drains to the river. The park remained part of the problem, just not the whole problem.

The volunteers shared their observations with local builders and the council. Some builders objected that the records did not identify which site had produced each piece of waste. Mei agreed and avoided accusing individual companies. Instead, she proposed better covers for storage areas and regular checks of nearby drains. Several companies joined a small trial, while the annual cleanup continued.

The following spring, the volunteers collected fewer bags. Attendance was similar, and the same stretch of river had been covered. This was encouraging, but Mei cautioned that rainfall had also been lower. She wanted another year's records before making a strong claim about the trial. The newspaper still printed a photograph, this time of volunteers sorting a smaller pile. Its caption explained why less trash could represent more progress.

readings.title: Who came after dark?
paragraphs: A city museum extended its Friday opening hours to attract people who could not visit during the day. The first evening event included live music and free admission. More than twice the usual number of visitors arrived, and the museum announced that the new hours had been a success. Yet one curator wanted to know whether those visitors were the people the change was intended to reach.

A short survey showed that many already visited regularly. They enjoyed the music and had invited friends who also had flexible schedules. People working late shifts were still poorly represented. Several said that the last bus from the museum left before their work ended. Others had not heard about the event because the advertising had mainly reached the museum's existing mailing list.

For the next series, the museum worked with local employers and placed posters at transport stops. It arranged a modest bus service from two workplaces and offered short tours that visitors could join without booking. The total attendance was lower than at the music event. However, a much larger share of visitors said it was their first museum visit in several years. Staff also noticed that these visitors asked different questions about the displays, prompting plans for new labels.

The museum did not stop holding concerts. They were enjoyable and helped raise money. It simply began reporting the two kinds of event separately. Large crowds and broader access were both valuable, but they were not interchangeable measures. The curator's question had not disproved the first event's success; it had clarified what kind of success it actually represented and what still needed to change.

readings.title: A better way to work
paragraphs: When a small design team missed an important deadline, its manager initially blamed a lack of effort. However, the team’s records told a different story. Several tasks had been assigned twice, while others had no clear owner. The manager decided to carry out a review before introducing longer working hours. Team members were encouraged to explain what had prevented them from making progress. Their feedback revealed that unclear instructions, rather than laziness, were the main obstacle. After responsibilities were clarified, the team completed its next project ahead of schedule. The manager learned that improving a process can be more effective than simply demanding more effort.

readings.title: The quiet experiment
paragraphs: A busy office introduced two hours of quiet work every morning. At first, several employees worried that communication would suffer. The team agreed to try the idea for one month and measure the results. People completed complex tasks faster, while urgent questions were collected for a short meeting at noon. The experiment did not eliminate collaboration; it gave collaboration a clearer place in the day. After the trial, the team voted to keep the new routine.

readings.title: The voice in the recording
paragraphs: When Mara found a recording of her grandmother describing life in a mining town, she expected it to settle a family disagreement. Her father remembered his childhood there as unusually secure; his younger sister recalled constant anxiety about money. The recording, made for a local history project, seemed at first to support the father's version. Their mother spoke warmly about neighbors sharing food and looking after one another's children. Mara began selecting extracts for a family gathering.

Listening again, she noticed how often the interviewer interrupted whenever the conversation approached wages or industrial disputes. He was interested in community traditions, and his questions steered the speaker back toward celebrations and mutual help. This did not make the grandmother's affectionate memories false. It did mean that the absence of complaints could not safely be treated as evidence that there had been nothing to complain about. The recording preserved a conversation shaped by two people, not a complete inventory of one person's experience.

Mara asked her aunt to listen before showing the edited version. Her aunt recognized every cheerful incident but supplied details that complicated them. Neighbors had shared food partly because some households could not afford enough. Looking after children had been generous, but it also allowed parents to work unpredictable shifts. The same event could be remembered as solidarity by one child and insecurity by another, without either memory being invented.

For the gathering, Mara included longer passages and left several of the interviewer's questions audible. She also invited both siblings to comment afterward. Her father worried that this would turn a celebration into an argument, but the discussion was gentler than he expected. Nobody withdrew their earlier account. Instead, they began to understand what each account had emphasized. Mara had hoped that the recording would deliver a verdict; it proved more valuable as a starting point for questions that the original interview had never asked.

readings.title: The recommendation she did not send
paragraphs: A former student asked Professor Hale for a recommendation for a research position. He had produced an excellent final project, but during the course he had also missed several deadlines. Hale remembered the frustration vividly and drafted a letter that praised his originality while warning that he needed close supervision. Before sending it, she checked the course records to make sure she was describing a pattern rather than an isolated incident.

The records confirmed the missed deadlines, but they also reminded her that the student had been caring for a sick parent. At the time, he had asked for an extension only once, apparently reluctant to explain the situation repeatedly. Hale had agreed to the extension and then mentally grouped the later delays with ordinary carelessness. Recognizing this did not tell her how dependable he would be in a demanding new role. It did, however, weaken the confidence with which she had been turning past behavior into a stable description of his character.

She contacted him to ask what the position involved and whether he was comfortable discussing the circumstances of that semester. He explained that the role included fixed laboratory shifts, that his care responsibilities had changed, and that he had recently completed an internship. With his permission, Hale spoke to the internship supervisor, who described him as punctual and careful about communicating possible delays. That report was encouraging but covered only a short period and a different kind of work.

Hale rewrote the recommendation. She gave specific examples of the student's analytical strengths, stated when she had taught him, and avoided predictions she could not justify. She did not disclose his family circumstances. The letter was less sweeping than her original draft, but also more informative. To recommend someone responsibly, she concluded, was neither to erase every reservation nor to transform a difficult semester into a permanent verdict. It was to distinguish what she had observed from what she had merely inferred.

readings.title: The price of an empty seat
paragraphs: The proposed closure of a night train divided a regional council. On paper, the service looked wasteful: several passenger cars ran half empty, and the fare revenue covered only a fraction of operating costs. Supporters responded with photographs of students, hospital staff, and elderly travelers who depended on the route. Both sides produced persuasive examples, but neither initially explained what would happen to those passengers if the train disappeared.

An independent transport team examined alternative journeys. Some travelers could switch to daytime trains with little inconvenience. Others would need an extra night in a hotel, miss a shift, or travel by car. For passengers attending early hospital appointments, the apparent replacement service arrived too late. The analysts also found that certain empty cars could be removed on quiet nights without eliminating the route. This would save less than closure, but more than keeping the schedule and train length unchanged.

The findings did not produce an obvious answer. Counting the cost of a missed shift required assumptions about whose time mattered and how it should be valued. The team made those assumptions explicit and published estimates under several different scenarios. Critics accused it of making the issue unnecessarily complicated. The lead analyst replied that the complications were already present in the journeys; the report had merely stopped hiding them inside a single financial total.

The council approved a reduced service for a year, alongside a booking system intended to match train length to likely demand. It promised to review both expenditure and the journeys people could still make. Campaigners welcomed the reprieve but worried that advance booking would disadvantage passengers whose work schedules changed on short notice. The council added a reserve allocation of seats. The compromise satisfied neither side completely. Yet it shifted the debate from whether an empty seat was inherently wasteful to which transport needs the region was prepared to support and at what cost.

readings.title: The sentence that would not travel
paragraphs: A publisher commissioned a new English translation of a novel famous for its spare, restrained dialogue. The translator, Inez, encountered a recurring expression that literally referred to leaving a door unlatched. In the original language, it could signal hospitality, reluctance to end an argument, or a refusal to make a final decision. No single English phrase carried all three associations naturally. Repeating the literal image would preserve a visible pattern but risk confusing readers about what the characters meant.

Inez initially chose a different English expression for each occurrence. Her sentences sounded natural, and individual conversations were easier to follow. During a later revision, however, she noticed that a connection between two distant scenes had vanished. Early in the novel, a mother used the expression to welcome her son home; near the end, he used it while postponing an answer to her request. The repeated wording made the second scene echo the first, with an emotional ambiguity that her varied translations had removed.

She experimented with retaining the door image in those two scenes while translating other occurrences more freely. An editor objected that this seemed inconsistent. Inez replied that consistency of wording was not the only kind of consistency a translation could pursue. Her aim was to preserve the relationship between scenes as well as the immediate sense of each line. The editor remained concerned that readers might notice a symbol the original audience would have encountered more casually.

The published version kept the two linked images and included a brief translator's note discussing the decision without proposing a single correct solution. Reviews disagreed about the result. One praised the echo; another found it slightly conspicuous. Inez regarded both reactions as useful evidence about the compromise she had made. Translation, in this instance, had not involved choosing between accuracy and freedom once and for all. It had required deciding which aspect of a sentence's work should be allowed to travel with it.

questions.question: Why was the recurring expression difficult to translate?
options: Its associations exceeded those of any single natural English equivalent
It referred to an unknown object
The translator did not know its literal meaning
questions.explanation: Problem dotyczył wielu skojarzeń, nie braku znajomości dosłownego znaczenia.
questions.evidence: No single English phrase carried all three associations naturally.

questions.question: What was lost in the first approach?
options: A meaningful echo between distant scenes
The immediate sense of every conversation
The order of the novel's events
questions.explanation: Naturalne lokalne tłumaczenia osłabiły powiązanie między scenami.
questions.evidence: a connection between two distant scenes had vanished.

questions.question: What did Inez mean by another kind of consistency?
options: Preserving relationships and effects rather than identical wording everywhere
questions.explanation: Spójność może dotyczyć funkcji i powiązań, nie tylko jednego odpowiednika słownego.
questions.evidence: preserve the relationship between scenes as well as the immediate sense of each line.

questions.question: What was the editor's remaining concern?
options: The novel had too few notes
The English image might draw more attention than the original did
Readers would not know what a door was
questions.explanation: Odtworzenie obrazu mogło zwiększyć jego wyrazistość względem oryginału.
questions.evidence: readers might notice a symbol the original audience would have encountered more casually.

questions.question: What does the final paragraph imply?
options: Freedom and accuracy can always be separated completely
A defensible translation can still involve visible losses and trade-offs
Critical disagreement proves a translation is worthless
questions.explanation: Sprzeczne recenzje ujawniają koszt świadomego kompromisu, nie automatyczną porażkę.
questions.evidence: useful evidence about the compromise she had made.

readings.title: The waiting list that grew shorter
paragraphs: A clinic introduced an online system designed to reduce the time patients spent waiting for routine appointments. Instead of being assigned the next available slot, patients could choose among cancellations that appeared throughout the day. Within two months, the average recorded wait had fallen. The clinic celebrated the result, and other services asked whether they could adopt the same software.

A receptionist noticed a less encouraging pattern. Patients who visited the booking page frequently found appointments quickly, while people without reliable internet access continued to call the clinic. Staff could book on their behalf, but the best openings were often gone by the time the telephone line was answered. The system had improved the allocation of some unused slots, yet it had also rewarded the ability to monitor a screen. The average concealed a widening difference between groups.

When the clinic examined the figures more closely, it discovered another complication. The waiting-time calculation began when a booking was successfully made, not when a patient first attempted to obtain one. Someone who spent a week checking the page before finding a slot could appear to have waited only a day. The old system had measured from the initial request. Comparing the two averages without mentioning that change had exaggerated the apparent improvement.

The clinic corrected its report and created a separate call-in list for patients who could not repeatedly check the website. Canceled appointments were divided between that call-in list and the online list. This made the headline average look slightly worse, even as access became more balanced. Some staff found the reversal embarrassing. The receptionist argued that the purpose was not to protect a number but to help patients get appointments. The revised system still saved useful time, but its success was now described through several measures, including unsuccessful booking attempts and differences between patient groups. Those figures were harder to summarize, yet considerably harder to mistake for the whole story.

questions.question: Who benefited most immediately from the new system?
options: Patients able to check the website frequently
Patients who could only call once a week
questions.explanation: Częste sprawdzanie strony dawało przewagę, więc korzyści nie rozkładały się równo.
questions.evidence: Patients who visited the booking page frequently found appointments quickly

questions.question: Why was the comparison with the old average misleading?
options: The old system had no waiting list
The clinic measured only emergency patients
The starting point of the measurement had changed
questions.explanation: Dawniej liczono od prośby; nowa miara pomijała czas szukania wolnego terminu.
questions.evidence: The old system had measured from the initial request.

questions.question: What did the new call-in list aim to address?
options: A legal ban on telephone bookings
Unequal ability to monitor online openings
The absence of any canceled appointments
questions.explanation: Nowa lista telefoniczna wspierała osoby, które nie mogły stale odświeżać strony.
questions.evidence: patients who could not repeatedly check the website.

questions.question: Why could a worse headline average accompany an improvement?
options: Fairer access was not fully represented by that average
questions.explanation: Jedna liczba nie oddaje całego celu: gorsza średnia może współistnieć z bardziej równym dostępem.
questions.evidence: made the headline average look slightly worse, even as access became more balanced.

questions.question: What is the receptionist's central argument?
options: Measures should serve the service's purpose rather than become its purpose
questions.explanation: Miernik ma pomagać oceniać usługę, a nie zastępować jej sens.
questions.evidence: the purpose was not to protect a number but to help patients get appointments.

readings.title: When efficiency becomes a habit
paragraphs: A logistics company replaced informal problem-solving with a detailed reporting system. The change initially improved accountability, because recurring failures became easier to trace. Over time, however, employees began documenting minor issues instead of resolving them immediately. Management eventually recognized that the procedure had become an end in itself. The company retained reports for serious incidents but restored individual discretion for routine decisions. This balance preserved useful evidence without discouraging initiative.

questions.question: What was the initial benefit of the system?
questions.explanation: System ułatwił ustalanie odpowiedzialności i śledzenie awarii.
questions.evidence: The change initially improved accountability, because recurring failures became easier to trace.

questions.question: What unintended behavior appeared?
questions.explanation: Pracownicy zaczęli opisywać drobiazgi zamiast je od razu rozwiązywać.
questions.evidence: employees began documenting minor issues instead of resolving them immediately.

questions.question: What solution was adopted?
questions.explanation: Przy rutynowych decyzjach przywrócono samodzielność.
questions.evidence: The company retained reports for serious incidents but restored individual discretion for routine decisions.

readings.title: The value of an unfinished answer
paragraphs: During a public debate, a researcher was asked to predict how a new technology would affect employment. Rather than offering a confident figure, she explained which evidence was still missing. Some listeners interpreted her caution as weakness, yet her answer changed the tone of the discussion. Other speakers began distinguishing established facts from assumptions. By the end, the audience had fewer simple predictions but a clearer understanding of the uncertainty involved. Intellectual honesty had made the debate more useful, not less decisive.

questions.question: What did the researcher refuse to provide?
questions.explanation: Nie podała pewnej liczby bez wystarczających danych.
questions.evidence: Rather than offering a confident figure, she explained which evidence was still missing.

questions.question: How did other speakers react?
questions.explanation: Zaczęli odróżniać fakty od założeń.
questions.evidence: Other speakers began distinguishing established facts from assumptions.

questions.question: What did the audience gain?
questions.explanation: Publiczność lepiej zrozumiała zakres niepewności.
questions.evidence: the audience had fewer simple predictions but a clearer understanding of the uncertainty involved.

readings.title: The perfectly unanimous meeting
paragraphs: The minutes of the committee's meeting recorded unanimous approval of the redevelopment plan. This was accurate in the narrowest procedural sense: when the chair finally called for objections, nobody spoke. It was also a remarkably efficient way of making the preceding two hours disappear. During that time, members had disputed the projected rents, the fate of several small businesses, and whether the promised public courtyard would remain public after dark. None of those disagreements survived into the single sentence that announced the decision.

Leonie, the committee's newest member, had asked for an estimate of displacement. The consultant explained that such an estimate would require information not yet available. When she suggested postponing approval until it was available, the chair reminded everyone that the application deadline was Friday. A delay, he said, would itself be a decision, with consequences for the neighborhood. This was not an unreasonable point. What troubled Leonie was that the same seriousness was not applied to the consequences of approving a proposal whose uncertainties remained unresolved.

By the final vote, two members had left for other commitments, one had been reassured by a promise of later consultation, and another was exhausted by the discussion. Leonie stayed silent because the chair had framed the motion as approval to continue negotiating, not approval of every detail. The published minutes, however, contained no such qualification. The developer subsequently cited them as evidence that the community's representatives endorsed the plan as presented.

Leonie requested a correction. She did not argue that the vote had never occurred or that the chair had deliberately falsified it. Her point was that a formally true record could nonetheless misrepresent what participants believed they had authorized. The committee eventually added a paragraph describing the outstanding questions. The developer called this an unnecessary complication; the chair called it clarification. Leonie accepted the latter term, though she suspected that clarification was often the name institutions gave to a disagreement once it had become too visible to omit.

At the next meeting, the committee approved a new practice: every motion would be read aloud in its final wording before a vote. It was a modest safeguard, not a guarantee of honest deliberation. Yet it made it slightly harder for silence to acquire a meaning that nobody had consciously chosen.

questions.question: How should the opening description of unanimity be understood?
options: Entirely fabricated because no vote occurred
Proof that all concerns had been resolved
Evidence that every member stayed until the end
questions.explanation: Prawdziwość zapisu proceduralnego nie oznacza wiernego oddania treści debaty.
questions.evidence: accurate in the narrowest procedural sense:

questions.question: What asymmetry troubled Leonie?
options: The deadline applied to some members only
The consultant knew every answer but refused to speak
Delay was scrutinized more seriously than the risks of premature approval
Only the developer was allowed to vote
questions.explanation: Leonie nie zaprzecza kosztom zwłoki; wskazuje nierówne traktowanie obu rodzajów ryzyka.
questions.evidence: the same seriousness was not applied to the consequences of approving a proposal

questions.question: Why did Leonie remain silent during the vote?
options: She did not know that redevelopment was being discussed
She understood the motion as permission to negotiate further
She accepted every detail of the proposal
questions.explanation: Jej milczenie opierało się na węższym rozumieniu tego, co zatwierdzano.
questions.evidence: approval to continue negotiating, not approval of every detail.

questions.question: What did her request for correction challenge?
options: The meaning attributed to a real procedural event
The developer's right to submit an application
Every statement the consultant had made
questions.explanation: Kwestionowała interpretację zapisu, nie fakt głosowania.
questions.evidence: a formally true record could nonetheless misrepresent what participants believed they had authorized.

questions.question: What is suggested by her reflection on 'clarification'?
options: The chair had admitted intentional fraud
Institutions may use a neutral term to absorb visible conflict
questions.explanation: To sceptyczna obserwacja o języku instytucji, nie dowód oszustwa ani całkowite odrzucenie protokołów.
questions.evidence: the name institutions gave to a disagreement once it had become too visible to omit.

questions.question: How does the final paragraph qualify the reform?
options: It removes the need for recorded votes
It reduces one risk without ensuring perfect deliberation
questions.explanation: Rozwiązanie ma ograniczoną, konkretną wartość; narrator unika obietnicy doskonałości.
questions.evidence: a modest safeguard, not a guarantee of honest deliberation.

readings.title: What the painting had become
paragraphs: The portrait had hung in the town hall for so long that its brownish varnish seemed inseparable from its identity. Generations of residents knew the sitter as a severe, almost spectral figure emerging from a dim background. When a conservator proposed cleaning it, the trustees assumed that the task was straightforward: remove what time had added and recover what the painter had intended. The conservator, Amélie, was less comfortable with that formulation. Some layers were later additions, but the boundary between damage, historical alteration, and deliberate revision was not equally clear everywhere.

Tests revealed a bright blue sleeve beneath the yellowed surface and a small landscape that had all but disappeared. They also suggested that part of the sitter's hand had been repainted decades after the original work. Removing that paint might expose an earlier gesture, but it could also disturb fragile material beneath it. The available evidence did not establish whether the repainting had repaired a loss or changed the composition to suit a later owner's taste. An old photograph offered tantalizing support for both interpretations, depending on how its blurred shadows were read.

At a public meeting, several residents objected to the prospect of a more colorful portrait. They understood that the brown tone was not original, yet they felt that cleaning would erase the image through which the town had remembered its benefactor. Others dismissed this concern as sentimentality. Amélie resisted that dismissal without treating familiarity as a reason to preserve every accumulated layer. The painting was simultaneously a material object, an artwork with a history of interventions, and a civic image shaped by repeated encounters.

The trustees approved limited cleaning, retained the uncertain repainting, and commissioned a display explaining the choices. The blue sleeve reappeared; the hand remained as residents knew it. Some critics called the result indecisive, as if a coherent treatment had to move uniformly toward a single past moment. Amélie described it instead as a decision about the strength of the evidence in different parts of the same object.

The restored portrait looked both familiar and unexpectedly vivid. It did not reveal an uncontested original hiding intact beneath dirt. It made visible how much of what people called the original depended on judgments about which changes to reverse, which to retain, and which uncertainties future conservators should be allowed to reconsider.

questions.question: What assumption did Amélie question?
options: That all later layers could be cleanly separated from a recoverable original
That the portrait was physically old
questions.explanation: Warstwy nie dawały się wszędzie jednoznacznie sklasyfikować.
questions.evidence: the boundary between damage, historical alteration, and deliberate revision was not equally clear everywhere.

questions.question: Why was the hand treated differently from the sleeve?
options: The evidence and risks differed between the two areas
The hand was not part of the painting
questions.explanation: Niepewność interpretacji oraz ryzyko uszkodzenia uzasadniały inny zakres ingerencji.
questions.evidence: Removing that paint might expose an earlier gesture, but it could also disturb fragile material beneath it.

questions.question: How did Amélie respond to residents' attachment?
options: She treated it as relevant without making it an absolute veto
She agreed that nothing should ever be cleaned
She claimed the brown varnish was original
questions.explanation: Uznała wagę znajomości obrazu, ale nie podporządkowała jej każdej decyzji.
questions.evidence: without treating familiarity as a reason to preserve every accumulated layer.

questions.question: What does the phrase 'a single past moment' criticize?
options: The possibility of dating a painting
The residents' knowledge of local history
Any attempt to study earlier images
The idea that coherent restoration must return every part to one chosen date
questions.explanation: Narrator kwestionuje utożsamienie spójności z jednolitym cofnięciem wszystkich zmian.
questions.evidence: as if a coherent treatment had to move uniformly toward a single past moment.

questions.question: What was a benefit of retaining the uncertain repainting?
options: It proved who had repainted the hand
questions.explanation: Zachowanie warstwy pozostawia otwartą możliwość późniejszej oceny.
questions.evidence: which uncertainties future conservators should be allowed to reconsider.

questions.question: Which statement best captures the passage's view of restoration?
options: It always requires complete removal of later paint
It involves evidence-based choices rather than simple recovery of a self-evident original
It should be determined entirely by public taste
It is impossible to improve any old artwork
questions.explanation: Restauracja wymaga interpretacji materiału i oceny dowodów, a nie jedynie mechanicznego odsłonięcia.
questions.evidence: how much of what people called the original depended on judgments

readings.title: The exception that became the rule
paragraphs: The software company's reliability report attributed a recent outage to an exceptional sequence of events. A routine update had coincided with an unusually large import, after which an automatic recovery process had exhausted the remaining capacity. Each event, considered separately, fell within the system's documented limits. Together they produced a failure that no single team believed it owned. The report was precise about timing and conspicuously vague about responsibility.

An engineer named Dev accepted that the combination was uncommon. What he questioned was the inference that uncommon meant unforeseeable, or that unforeseeable meant nobody could have prepared for it. The teams had optimized their own components under assumptions about the behavior of neighboring components. Those assumptions were reasonable in isolation but had never been tested together under pressure. The recovery process, praised in earlier reviews for its persistence, kept retrying work that the overloaded system needed it to stop attempting.

Dev proposed a simulation in which several individually acceptable conditions occurred simultaneously. A manager worried that such tests would be expensive and could generate endless scenarios without a clear stopping point. Dev agreed that exhaustive prediction was impossible. His purpose was not to imagine every future accident, but to identify where the system lacked a way to fail gradually. A component that could temporarily refuse work might look less accommodating in a local performance chart while making the overall service more dependable.

The team eventually introduced limits on automatic retries and a controlled mode that postponed nonessential imports during overload. Customer support helped write messages explaining what was delayed and what remained available. In the next incident, some customers still experienced disruption, and the monthly report did not describe the outcome as flawless. The crucial difference was that the disruption remained contained rather than spreading until the entire service stopped.

At the review meeting, the phrase 'exceptional circumstances' appeared again. This time it introduced the conditions the system had handled imperfectly, not an argument for treating those conditions as outside its designers' concern. Dev regarded that linguistic change as significant, though hardly sufficient. An organization could adopt the vocabulary of resilience while continuing to reward only uninterrupted local performance. Whether the lesson endured would depend on what teams were allowed to sacrifice when the next set of targets was negotiated.

questions.question: What is the implied criticism of the original report?
options: It contained no details about the failure
Technical precision coexisted with avoidance of shared responsibility
It blamed a single customer without evidence
questions.explanation: Kontrast sugeruje, że dokładność techniczna nie zastąpiła odpowiedzi na pytanie o odpowiedzialność.
questions.evidence: precise about timing and conspicuously vague about responsibility.

questions.question: What chain of assumptions did Dev challenge?
options: That rare events are necessarily unforeseeable and therefore beyond preparation
That every event can be predicted exactly
That all updates are inherently dangerous
That customers should never import data
questions.explanation: Dev rozdziela rzadkość, przewidywalność i możliwość ograniczania skutków.
questions.evidence: uncommon meant unforeseeable, or that unforeseeable meant nobody could have prepared for it.

questions.question: Why had the recovery process become harmful?
options: It stopped after the first attempt
Its repeated attempts consumed capacity during overload
questions.explanation: Zwykle ceniona uporczywość pogłębiła przeciążenie.
questions.evidence: kept retrying work that the overloaded system needed it to stop attempting.

questions.question: What was the aim of the proposed simulation?
options: To prove that local targets were always useless
To reveal weaknesses in containing failure
questions.explanation: Celem było kontrolowanie degradacji, a nie wszechwiedza o przyszłych awariach.
questions.evidence: identify where the system lacked a way to fail gradually.

questions.question: How did the next incident differ?
options: Disruption was limited instead of spreading across the service
questions.explanation: Poprawa polegała na ograniczeniu zasięgu, nie pełnym wyeliminowaniu zakłóceń.
questions.evidence: the disruption remained contained rather than spreading

questions.question: What reservation does the final paragraph express?
options: New language matters little unless incentives allow the corresponding trade-offs
The vocabulary change guarantees future reliability
All performance targets must be abolished
questions.explanation: Trwałość zmiany zależy od realnych zasad oceny i dopuszczalnych kompromisów.
questions.evidence: what teams were allowed to sacrifice when the next set of targets was negotiated.

readings.title: A guide to getting lost
paragraphs: The review copy arrived with a promise on its cover: a city guide that would help visitors escape the itinerary. Its author recommended unnamed alleys, unadvertised courtyards, and cafes supposedly untouched by tourism. The reviewer, Celia, found the photographs beautiful and the premise faintly self-defeating. Once a secluded courtyard appeared in a widely distributed guide, its seclusion became something the book was both celebrating and helping to undo. This did not make the recommendation dishonest, but it complicated the claim that readers could purchase an unmediated encounter with the city.

Celia followed one suggested walk. The route led through a residential district where a baker greeted regular customers by name and a delivery driver temporarily blocked the narrow street. Nothing dramatic happened. At the recommended cafe, she met three people carrying the same guide. They laughed at the coincidence, then lowered their voices as though their shared wish to avoid tourists required them to conceal their own presence. Celia wondered whether the book had offered escape from tourism or merely a more flattering role within it.

Yet she was reluctant to turn the review into a performance of superiority. Without the guide, she would probably never have visited that district, and the cafe owner seemed pleased with the extra customers. Nor did the residents exist to supply outsiders with an atmosphere of authentic everyday life. A place was not spoiled simply because a stranger learned how to reach it. The difficulty lay in the expectation that it should remain unchanged for the benefit of successive visitors who each imagined themselves unusually perceptive.

Her review praised the practical maps and criticized the rhetoric of discovery. The guide was useful when it admitted to being a guide; it became less convincing when it presented its own recommendations as a release from recommendation itself. Celia suggested reading it as an invitation to pay attention, not as a certificate that one's experiences were more genuine than those of people on a sightseeing bus.

The publisher quoted the phrase 'an invitation to pay attention' in its publicity, leaving out the qualification. Celia was irritated, then amused. Her carefully balanced review had supplied another compact promise for the cover. The city would continue changing regardless, but the appetite for instructions on how to encounter it without instructions appeared remarkably durable.

questions.question: Why does Celia find the premise self-defeating?
options: Publicizing secluded places can alter the quality being advertised
The author refuses to recommend cafes
questions.explanation: Popularny poradnik może osłabiać odosobnienie, które poleca jako zaletę.
questions.evidence: its seclusion became something the book was both celebrating and helping to undo.

questions.question: What is implied by the visitors lowering their voices?
options: The owner has ordered absolute silence
They are planning to leave without paying
They feel an awkward tension between their self-image and their shared tourist behavior
questions.explanation: Gest pokazuje napięcie między byciem turystą a pragnieniem odróżnienia się od turystów.
questions.evidence: their shared wish to avoid tourists required them to conceal their own presence.

questions.question: Why does Celia resist simply condemning the guide?
options: She thinks all advertised claims are accurate
It has practical value and residents are not obliged to remain unchanged
She believes the publisher will pay her more
questions.explanation: Nie utożsamia odkrycia miejsca przez gości z automatycznym zniszczeniem jego wartości.
questions.evidence: A place was not spoiled simply because a stranger learned how to reach it.

questions.question: What distinction underlies her review?
options: All independent travel is better than bus travel
Practical guidance differs from a claim to certify authentic experience
Maps are always superior to photographs
Local cafes should never accept strangers
questions.explanation: Poradnik może pomagać obserwować, ale nie uprawnia do uznawania własnych przeżyć za bardziej autentyczne.
questions.evidence: an invitation to pay attention, not as a certificate

questions.question: What is ironic about the publisher's quotation?
options: A criticism of simplified promises becomes another simplified promise
The publisher quotes a sentence not in the review
Celia had demanded that every word be removed
The quotation makes the guide unusable
questions.explanation: Wycięty z kontekstu komplement powiela mechanizm, który recenzja problematyzowała.
questions.evidence: Her carefully balanced review had supplied another compact promise for the cover.

questions.question: Which description best fits Celia's stance?
options: Certain that she alone travels authentically
Critical but aware that she is implicated in the same contradictions
questions.explanation: Samokrytycyzm chroni ją przed przedstawieniem siebie jako wyjątku od opisywanego zjawiska.
questions.evidence: she was reluctant to turn the review into a performance of superiority.

readings.title: The unwritten contract
paragraphs: For nearly twenty years, a small bakery had supplied bread to the community hall at a price barely above cost. There was no written agreement. The arrangement had begun when the hall's former caretaker helped the bakery survive a flood, and both parties had gradually come to regard it as ordinary. New volunteers knew the discount existed but not how it had originated. The baker, Tomas, rarely mentioned the history; he was proud of the connection and uncomfortable making generosity sound like a debt.

When flour and energy costs rose, Tomas told the hall's new treasurer that he would need to increase the price. She compared his proposed rate with two larger suppliers and found it still competitive, though no longer exceptionally cheap. At the committee meeting, however, several volunteers described the increase as a withdrawal of support. One suggested that the bakery had benefited for years from the hall's recommendations and therefore owed it a continued concession. Tomas, who had not been invited to that discussion, heard the remark through a customer.

His first impulse was to end the arrangement. What hurt was not the negotiation over price but the transformation of something he had chosen to give into something others claimed the right to demand. The treasurer recognized a different problem. She had inherited a budget dependent on an informal subsidy whose conditions nobody had documented. Treating the old price as permanent had made the hall's finances appear more secure than they were. Neither the bakery nor the volunteers had deliberately concealed this fragility, but everyone had found it convenient not to name it.

She invited Tomas to meet two committee members. They agreed on a price reviewed annually, with a small additional donation from the bakery for one particular event. The distinction mattered: ordinary purchases would be paid for as purchases, and support would be described as support. Some volunteers regretted the loss of an arrangement that had seemed warmer precisely because it was unwritten. Tomas shared a little of that regret, yet he no longer wanted warmth to depend on his absorbing costs that others did not see.

The new agreement did not exhaust the relationship. Tomas still sent extra rolls when an event attracted more people than expected, and the volunteers still recommended his shop. What changed was the presumption that kindness, once repeated often enough, ceased to be a choice. Putting part of the relationship in writing had not necessarily diminished trust; it had removed one way in which trust could quietly become obligation.

questions.question: Why had the original arrangement become vulnerable to misunderstanding?
options: The bakery had always charged the highest price
The hall had a detailed permanent contract
Tomas had publicly demanded repayment after the flood
Its history and conditions were no longer shared knowledge
questions.explanation: Znano cenę, ale nie okoliczności ani warunki powstania ustalenia.
questions.evidence: New volunteers knew the discount existed but not how it had originated.

questions.question: What particularly hurt Tomas?
options: The hall had stopped buying bread years earlier
His new price was above every competitor's
A voluntary contribution was being treated as an entitlement
questions.explanation: Uraziło go roszczeniowe przeformułowanie dobrowolnego gestu, nie sama rozmowa o kosztach.
questions.evidence: something he had chosen to give into something others claimed the right to demand.

questions.question: What financial weakness did the treasurer identify?
options: The volunteers had deliberately falsified accounts
The budget relied on an undocumented subsidy assumed to be permanent
The hall had no customers at any event
The bakery was charging twice the agreed rate
questions.explanation: Nieformalna pomoc została potraktowana jak stabilny element finansowania.
questions.evidence: a budget dependent on an informal subsidy whose conditions nobody had documented.

questions.question: Why was the separate event donation significant?
options: It distinguished a commercial price from a chosen act of support
It restored the old discount on every order
It required Tomas to donate indefinitely
questions.explanation: Nazwanie dwóch rodzajów relacji zapobiega myleniu zapłaty z darowizną.
questions.evidence: ordinary purchases would be paid for as purchases, and support would be described as support.

questions.question: How is the nostalgia for the unwritten arrangement qualified?
options: All volunteers had knowingly exploited Tomas
Tomas had never valued the connection
Its apparent warmth concealed costs borne unevenly
questions.explanation: Tekst uznaje emocjonalną wartość dawnej relacji, ale pokazuje niewidoczny koszt po jednej stronie.
questions.evidence: warmth to depend on his absorbing costs that others did not see.

questions.question: What does the ending suggest about formal agreements?
options: They guarantee that costs will never rise
They eliminate the need for communication
They can protect voluntary generosity by clarifying obligations

readings.title: The value of leaving a question open
paragraphs: When a coastal town commissioned an assessment of its flood defenses, officials expected a single, unequivocal recommendation. The engineers instead supplied several scenarios, each contingent on assumptions about future rainfall and land use. Some council members construed this caution as evidence of incompetence. Yet the report's apparent indecision was precisely what made it useful: it distinguished observations from conjecture. A cheaper barrier would suffice under current conditions but could channel floodwater toward neighboring communities if development continued upstream. Rather than endorse a supposedly definitive solution, the council funded reversible improvements and annual reassessments. The decision attracted criticism for lacking ambition. A decade later, however, its flexibility allowed the town to adapt without dismantling an expensive monument to outdated assumptions.

readings.title: An archive that tells two stories
paragraphs: A museum acquired a merchant's meticulously kept notebooks and initially presented them as an impartial record of commercial life. Prices, quantities, and destinations appeared to offer unusually solid evidence. A visiting historian nevertheless questioned what the notebooks left out. The merchant recorded purchased goods but seldom named the laborers who produced them, and losses were attributed to weather even when correspondence suggested deliberate neglect. These omissions did not render the archive worthless. They made it necessary to read the notebooks alongside other accounts and to treat their categories as historical choices rather than neutral facts. The revised exhibition retained the original figures but explained whose experiences those figures could not represent. Visitors consequently encountered both the merchant's account and an account of how historical knowledge is assembled.
